title: Common Manufacturing Processes in Detail
description: The named wasting, shaping, forming, additive, joining and finishing processes — tools, steps and safety.
content_html:
From Type to Technique

The specification requires you to know the specific named processes within each type — their tools, the steps involved, and the safety measures that must be followed. OCR exam questions regularly ask you to name a specific process, describe the steps, and justify why it suits a particular material or product.

Wasting Processes

Nine wasting processes are specified. Sawing uses a toothed blade to cut stock to length; workpieces must be clamped and PPE worn. Shearing (manual guillotine or tin snips only) cuts sheet metal with opposing blades — fast, no heat, but fingers must stay clear. Drilling uses a twist bit in a pillar drill; work is clamped, speed matched to the material, and swarf cleared regularly. Filing removes small amounts of material to refine surfaces; the workpiece is held in a vice and the file must have a handle fitted to prevent the tang injuring the hand.

Threading is restricted to manually cutting internal threads with a tap and external threads with a die; cutting paste is applied and the tool reversed every half turn to break swarf. Routing uses a rotating cutter for profiles and slots; dust extraction and guards are required. Laser cutting vaporises material along a programmed path with a high-energy beam — highly precise, minimal kerf, but requires interlocked enclosures and fume extraction. Turning on a centre lathe rotates the workpiece against a fixed cutting tool to reduce diameter; loose clothing must be secured. Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter on flat or contoured surfaces; CNC milling achieves complex shapes accurately and repeatedly.

Key Fact

The nine wasting processes in the specification are: sawing, shearing (manual guillotine/tin snips only), drilling, filing, threading (tap and die only), routing, laser cutting, turning, and milling. Each generates waste swarf or offcuts and requires appropriate PPE and clamping.

Shaping Processes

Sand casting packs sand around a split pattern in a two-part mould, pours molten metal into the cavity, then breaks away the sand to reveal the casting — suits large, complex shapes at low-to-medium volume. Die casting forces molten metal under pressure into a permanent hardened steel die, giving high dimensional accuracy and surface finish at high volume. Key difference: sand casting = single-use expendable mould; die casting = permanent reusable die. Injection moulding melts thermoplastic granules and injects the melt into a cooled steel mould; on solidification the mould opens and ejects the part — suits very high volumes of complex plastic components. Powder metallurgy compacts ceramic or metal powder at very high pressure then sinters (heats without fully melting) to bond particles — used for ceramic products and porous components such as self-lubricating bearings.

Sand casting uses an expendable (single-use) sand mould — once the metal solidifies, the mould is broken apart, so a new mould is needed for every part. This suits one-off and batch production of large, complex parts such as engine blocks. Die casting uses a permanent hardened steel die reused thousands of times; cycle times are very short, making it cost-effective at high volume, with far superior dimensional accuracy and surface finish. Remember: sand = expendable/single-use; die = permanent/reusable.

Forming Processes

Forging compresses hot metal between shaped dies, aligning the grain structure to produce a strong, tough component — spanners, crankshafts, aerospace fittings. Press forming blanks and bends sheet metal between punch and die — car body panels, casings and brackets. Strip heating softens a thermoplastic sheet along a line using a resistance heater (line bender) so it can be folded to a precise angle. Vacuum forming clamps a thermoplastic sheet over a mould, heats it until pliable, then draws it onto the mould by removing air; moulds need 3–5° draft angles for release, and surface detail reproduces on the mould-contact face only. Moulding of composite materials lays reinforcing fibres (glass or carbon cloth) in a mould, saturates them with liquid resin, and cures the assembly — used for boat hulls, sports equipment and aerospace panels.

Key Fact

Vacuum forming moulds must have draft angles (typically 3–5°) to allow the formed polymer sheet to be released. Deep draws with vertical walls cannot be vacuum formed because the sheet would lock onto the mould.

Additive Manufacturing

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) melts a thermoplastic filament (PLA or ABS) in a heated nozzle and deposits it layer by layer; the platform lowers by one layer after each pass. Slicing software converts the digital model into cross-sections and adds support structures automatically; supports are removed after printing. Tools: FDM printer, slicing software, filament spool. Safety: nozzle temperature 200–260 °C — avoid contact; ventilate to remove fumes.

Joining and Finishing Processes

Brazing melts a filler metal between closely fitting parts using a gas torch, WITHOUT melting the base metals themselves (only the filler melts — unlike welding); the filler flows by capillary action and solidifies on cooling — used for pipework, cycle frames and tool tips. PPE: face shield, heat-resistant gloves, ventilation. MIG/MAG welding feeds consumable wire electrode with a shielding gas (argon for MIG; CO₂/mix for MAG) to fuse steel; PPE: welding helmet, gloves, leather apron, ventilation. Riveting: hammered rivets are set with a hammer and dolly; pop rivets are installed from one side only using a rivet gun, suited to hollow sections. Mechanical fastening: nuts and bolts pass through clearance holes (removable); self-tapping screws cut their own thread in a pilot hole. Painting applies pigmented liquid by brush or spray to a clean, primed substrate. Powder coating electrostatically charges dry polymer powder onto an earthed component and cures it at 160–200 °C, giving a tough corrosion-resistant film without solvents.

Ask four questions to choose the right joining method. Are both parts metal? Brazing and MIG welding suit metals; nuts and bolts suit mixed materials. Must the joint be permanent? Welding and brazing are permanent; bolts and self-tapping screws allow disassembly. Is only one side accessible? Pop rivets are the answer. How heavy is the load? MIG welding gives the strongest bond; a self-tapping screw suits light-duty assembly only. Apply this checklist to every OCR scenario question on joining.
exam_tip_html: When asked to 'recommend with justification the most appropriate process', name the specific process (e.g. 'MIG welding'), state the process type (joining), and then give two linked reasons: one about the material or product requirement, and one about volume or practicality. Avoid vague phrases like 'it is good for metal' — instead write 'MIG welding produces a strong fusion weld in steel sheet, making it suitable for the structural chassis where high tensile loads are expected.' Always check whether the question restricts threading to tap and die or shearing to manual guillotine — if so, do not name power equivalents.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nine wasting processes (sawing, shearing, drilling, filing, threading, routing, laser cutting, turning, milling) all remove material; shearing is manual only (guillotine/tin snips) and threading is manual only (tap and die) on this specification.
  • Shaping processes (sand casting, die casting, injection moulding, powder metallurgy) pour or inject material into a mould — sand casting uses an expendable mould while die casting uses a permanent reusable steel die.
  • Process selection depends on material, volume, required accuracy, and cost — always justify your recommendation using at least two of these criteria in exam answers.

glossary_terms.definition: A wasting process that uses a toothed blade to cut through material along a straight or curved line.
A cutting tool used to produce an internal screw thread inside a drilled hole, used manually in the threading process.
A welding process using a continuous consumable wire electrode and a shielding gas to join metals by melting the joint.
A forming process in which reinforcing fibres are laid into a mould and saturated with resin, which cures to form a stiff composite part.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a shaping process?
A) Turning
B) Forging
C) Sand casting
D) Powder coating
State two safety measures that must be followed when using a pillar drill.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: clamp the workpiece securely to the table / wear safety glasses / keep loose clothing and hair away from the drill / select the correct speed for the material / clear swarf with a brush not fingers / lower the guard before drilling. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why die casting is more suitable than sand casting for producing 50,000 identical aluminium components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that die casting uses a permanent reusable steel die; 1 mark for explaining that this makes unit cost low at high volume; 1 mark for a developed point such as die casting achieves better dimensional accuracy and surface finish than sand casting, reducing finishing costs — or that the high initial die cost is amortised over 50,000 units, giving a lower cost per part than making a new sand mould for each casting. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the steps involved in the FDM 3D printing process. Include the tools and equipment required.
practice_questions.marks: Steps (up to 2 marks): slice the digital model in software into layers; load filament spool; FDM printer melts filament in heated nozzle; deposits material layer by layer onto build platform; platform lowers by one layer after each pass; support structures removed after printing (2 marks for a logical sequence covering at least three steps; 1 mark for a basic description). Equipment (up to 2 marks): FDM 3D printer, slicing software, thermoplastic filament spool (e.g. PLA or ABS); optionally: removal tools for supports (2 marks for naming at least two items; 1 mark for one). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is deciding between MIG welding and bolted mechanical fastening to join the steel side panels of a heavy-duty storage cabinet.

Discuss the factors that should influence this choice of joining method.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two factors from each process with specific reasoning. For example: MIG welding produces a strong permanent joint suitable for the structural load, gives a clean appearance, but requires skilled operators and PPE and cannot be disassembled for repair; bolting allows disassembly for maintenance or replacement, requires less skill, but creates stress concentrations at bolt holes and may loosen under vibration. A clear recommendation is reached with justification linked to the storage cabinet scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two factors identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors mentioned with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student is planning to manufacture a prototype housing for an electronic sensor. The housing has a complex curved outer surface and a hollow interior.

Evaluate the suitability of vacuum forming and FDM 3D printing for manufacturing this prototype, and justify which process you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation covering vacuum forming (suits curved surfaces, fast cycle, low cost per part, but requires a mould and cannot produce hollow interiors in one operation, draft angles limit deep vertical walls) and FDM (builds hollow complex geometry directly from the digital model, no tooling cost, but slower, lower surface finish, limited material choice). Judgement should favour FDM for a one-off prototype with complex hollow geometry because no mould cost, digital iteration is fast, and accuracy is adequate for a sensor housing. Judgement should be substantiated and acknowledge counterpoints.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two relevant points on each process and an attempted recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points identified but largely one-sided or without justification.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which two shearing tools are permitted in the OCR R041 specification?
In die casting, what type of mould is used?
Vacuum forming moulds must have _____ to allow the formed polymer sheet to be removed from the mould after cooling.
In FDM 3D printing, the thermoplastic _____ is melted in a heated nozzle and deposited layer by layer onto the build platform.
Match each joining process to its key characteristic.
right: Uses a filler metal melted by a gas torch; joins by capillary action
Only requires access from one side of the joint
Uses a consumable wire electrode with a shielding gas

flashcard_questions.q: In the OCR spec, threading is restricted to which tools?
flashcard_questions.a: Threading in the OCR specification is restricted to manually cutting threads using a tap for internal threads and a die for external threads.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between sand casting and die casting moulds?
flashcard_questions.a: Sand casting uses a single-use expendable sand mould, while die casting uses a permanent reusable hardened steel die.

flashcard_questions.q: What safety measure is most critical when using a pillar drill?
flashcard_questions.a: The workpiece must be clamped securely to the machine table to prevent it spinning and causing injury during drilling.

flashcard_questions.q: What are draft angles on a vacuum forming mould?
flashcard_questions.a: Draft angles are slight tapers (typically 3–5°) on mould walls that allow the formed polymer sheet to be released after cooling.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is laser cutting classified as a wasting process?
flashcard_questions.a: Laser cutting vaporises material along the cut path, removing it from the workpiece and generating waste fumes and kerf material.

flashcard_questions.q: What shielding gas does MIG welding use?
flashcard_questions.a: MIG welding uses an inert shielding gas such as argon to protect the weld pool from atmospheric contamination during fusion.

flashcard_questions.q: When is a pop rivet preferred over a hammered rivet?
flashcard_questions.a: A pop rivet is preferred when only one side of the joint is accessible, as it is set entirely from the front using a rivet gun.

flashcard_questions.q: What temperature range does FDM 3D printing typically use to melt PLA or ABS filament?
flashcard_questions.a: FDM 3D printing melts thermoplastic filament at nozzle temperatures typically between 200 °C and 260 °C depending on the material.

flashcard_questions.q: How does powder coating differ from spray painting?
flashcard_questions.a: Powder coating applies dry charged polymer powder electrostatically and cures it in an oven, producing a tougher film without solvents.

flashcard_questions.q: What does forging do to the grain structure of a metal component?
flashcard_questions.a: Forging aligns the grain structure of the metal along the component's profile, increasing its strength and toughness significantly.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four shaping processes listed in the OCR R041 specification.
flashcard_questions.a: The four shaping processes are sand casting, die casting, injection moulding, and powder metallurgy for ceramic products.

flashcard_questions.q: What is strip heating used for in polymer manufacture?
flashcard_questions.a: Strip heating softens a thermoplastic sheet along a narrow line using a line bender so that it can be folded to a precise angle.
